News.title: Daniel Kinahan has his own landing inside Irish prison where 'ongoing battle' rages
News.content:
Daniel Kinahan has his own landing inside Irish prison where 'ongoing battle' rages

Daniel Kinahan has been extradited from the UAE and is now remanded in custody at Portlaoise Prison in Ireland after being charged with leading a criminal organisation

View 6 Images Daniel Kinahan woke up in an Irish prison this morning (Image: Supplied)

Daniel Kinahan has set foot on Irish soil for the first time in a decade — and he is now having his first full day in an Irish jail where he has an entire landing to himself.

The alleged crime boss, 49, was extradited from the United Arab Emirates before being immediately detained upon touching down at Baldonnel Airfield in Dublin. He was brought before the Special Criminal Court — Ireland's non-jury court that handles serious organised crime and terrorism cases — where he faced charges of heading a criminal organisation between October 2015 and April 2017.

Dressed in a black tracksuit, Kinahan, who is originally from Dublin, was told that any bail applications would need to be made to the High Court. He replied: "I think we know I won't be getting bail — but thank you so much for explaining that."

He has now been remanded in custody at Portlaoise Prison, with his next court appearance scheduled for October. Should he be convicted, he faces up to 30 years behind bars.

View 6 Images Daniel Kinahan (back, right) leaving the Criminal Courts of Justice in Dublin, where he was remanded in custody charged with directing an organised crime group (Image: Mark Marlow/PA Wire)

So what exactly can Kinahan expect from life inside Ireland's only maximum security prison?

Located in County Laois, roughly an hour's drive south-west of Dublin, Portlaoise Prison houses some of the Republic's most dangerous and high-profile inmates.

The facility holds up to 226 prisoners and has long been the destination of choice for those convicted in connection with serious organised crime — including a number of Kinahan's own associates.

Among them is Sean McGovern, widely described as Kinahan's right-hand man. McGovern was injured during the notorious Regency Hotel attack in Dublin in 2016 — a gangland shooting that triggered a bloody feud between the Kinahan cartel and the rival Hutch gang, leaving more than a dozen people dead.

McGovern, who Kinahan will not be able to interact with, was the first person to be extradited to Ireland from the UAE in connection with the investigation, and pleaded guilty to directing a criminal organisation. He is currently serving his sentence at Portlaoise.

View 6 Images Reports suggest Kinahan will be given a landing to himself (Image: Irish Prison Service)

Kinahan, however, will not be rubbing shoulders with his former associates in the usual sense.

According to reports, a wing that typically houses eight prisoners has been cleared specifically for him. The Irish Mirror say he is on suicide watch and is being monitored 24 hours a day on a landing where he is completely separated from all other prisoners in the jail.

He is expected to spend up to 20 hours a day confined to his cell.

According to reports, he is now on suicide watch and will have to be watched 24 hours a day, and while he is secluded from other inmates, he will have a TV and access to things like Netflix.

Outside his cell, the prison has struggled with serious problems that will make for uncomfortable reading for anyone heading through its gates.

In December, criminologist John Cuffee, who previously worked at the facility, warned that drugs remain a persistent problem.

He told Midlands 103 radio: "A lot of prisoners want to get cured. They want their drug problems put behind them — they will do their best. If we can't keep drugs out of the country and out of your nightclub, your local pub, it is going to manifest in prisons. But it is an ongoing battle, and it is a battle prison staff will face and deal with as it comes up."

View 6 Images A general view of Portlaoise Prison in Co Laois (Image: PA)

Drug seizures at Portlaoise did fall in 2024, with 22 reported incidents — a 55% drop from the 48 recorded the previous year, according to the Irish Penal Reform Trust.

But staff have raised concerns about the methods being used to get contraband inside. Prison officers warned last year that drones were being used to deliver drugs, mobile phones and weapons directly into the jail, with fears that firearms could be among the cargo.

‌



Gabriel Keavney, deputy general secretary of the Prison Officer's Association, said: "There have been over 100 drone deliveries since the beginning of the year. We know there's drugs, we know there's phones, but we're very concerned they may also contain firearms. There's huge concerns for our members."

The authorities have attempted to tackle the problem. Justice minister Jim O'Callaghan announced that wire netting around the prison was being upgraded to steel netting to disrupt drone drops.

View 6 Images Daniel Kinahan has been a wanted man for years

‌



But Keavney said smugglers had already adapted: "What they've done since the steel netting was installed in Portlaoise, they delivered directly to the prison through the ventilation system — so it's impossible to net the entire prison."

The scale of the problem was thrown into sharp relief in 2024 when ten inmates were rushed to hospital after a mass overdose involving a white powder believed to be a synthetic drug that had been smuggled into the facility, leaving several people in a critical condition.

A Prison Officers Association spokesperson said at the time: "Unfortunately we have been saying for some time that the prisons are awash with drugs and no action has been taken by management."

‌



The Irish Prison Service insisted that tackling contraband remained a top priority, saying it had invested in new technology, increased cell searches and was working closely with the Garda Siochana — Ireland's national police force — at both local and national level to prevent items being smuggled in.

Violence has also been a recurring theme at the prison. In early 2023, a drink-fuelled New Year's celebration on one of the landings descended into a brawl.

View 6 Images Portlaoise Prison, Co Laois (Image: PA Images)

‌



Among those said to be involved was Aaron Brady, who was convicted in Ireland in 2020 of the murder of Garda detective Joe Fox — a case that drew significant attention in both Ireland and the UK. Brady was reportedly facing sanctions that would have seen his privileges — including access to the prison shop, phone calls and visits — curtailed as a result.

One of the more surreal episodes in the prison's history came in 2007, when armed robber John Daly managed to call into Liveline — a popular daytime phone-in show on Ireland's national broadcaster RTE — using a smuggled mobile phone.

The stunt caused considerable embarrassment and triggered searches that turned up more than 1,000 contraband items across the cells. Daly was transferred to other prisons before eventually being released — though he was fatally shot later that same year while travelling in a taxi in the Dublin suburb of Finglas.

Article continues below

For Kinahan, the contrast with life in Dubai — where he was understood to have enjoyed luxury properties, access to the boxing world and the trappings of serious wealth — could hardly be more stark.

In 2024, Portlaoise Prison grabbed headlines not just across Ireland, but in the UK as well, after 10 individuals were rushed to hospital following a mass "synthetic drug" overdose. The white powder was believed to have been smuggled into the prison, leaving several people in critical condition.

The Irish Prison Service stated that preventing drugs from entering prison was a top priority, adding in a lengthy statement: "The Irish Prison Service has committed to continuing to invest in new technologies and measures to support our efforts to keep contraband out of prisons.

News.title: UK weather maps show heatwave hitting 39C with 12 counties at 38C or more – list
News.content:
UK weather maps show heatwave hitting 39C with 12 counties at 38C or more – list

Weather models suggest this week’s heatwave could reach a staggering 39C as Met Office forecasters consider issuing amber or red extreme heat warnings

View 3 Images Anomaly maps show temperatures rising well above the seasonal average on Thursday (Image: WXCHARTS)

The UK faces its fifth heatwave of the year this week as weather models suggest temperatures could peak as high as 39C.

‌



Met Office forecasters are considering issuing amber or red extreme heat warnings ahead of what could be the hottest day of the year on Thursday. The current temperature record for 2026 stands at 37.7C, which came on June 26 in Lingwood, Norfolk.

‌



Temperatures are expected to peak at 29C today and 30C tomorrow, before surging into the mid-30s from Wednesday. The GFS model shows highs of 36C are on the cards in western parts of England on Wednesday.

‌



View 3 Images Maximum possible temperatures (C) at 6pm on Wednesday (Image: WXCHARTS)

UK weather maps turn volcanic red as new heatwave brings temperatures up to 39C READ MORE :

UK weather record on verge of being broken as Brits head for 'unprecedented' fifth heatwave of 2026 READ MORE :

Much of the south could reach 35C, with South Wales hitting 33C, the Midlands reaching 34C, and areas as far north as Yorkshire rising to 33C. Temperatures are expected to be a fair few notches cooler in Northern Ireland and Scotland.

Thursday should be the hottest day this week. The GFS model shows scorching 39C highs are possible in Gloucestershire, with 38C potentially coming quite widely in western and southern parts of England.

‌



Temperature anomaly maps for Thursday show England and Wales shaded in black. This indicates where temperatures will rise well above the seasonal average for this time of year.

View 3 Images Maximum possible temperatures (C) at 6pm on Thursday (Image: WXCHARTS)

‌



In total, the GFS model maps suggest 12 counties could reach 38C or more on Thursday. They are all in England.

UK counties facing 38C or more

Shropshire

Hereford

Worcestershire

Gloucestershire

Warwickshire

Staffordshire

Oxfordshire

Buckinghamshire

Berkshire

Wiltshire

Hampshire

Northamptonshire

Met Office weather forecast

The Met Office has said it is considering issuing amber or red extreme heat warnings as temperatures climb into the mid to high-30s later this week.

‌



“We’ll probably see highs reaching the mid-30s quite widely on Wednesday, and indeed on Thursday too for England and Wales,” Met Office meteorologist Tom Morgan said.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

“On Wednesday, probably the Midlands, maybe a little bit further south, the M4 corridor, west of London, up towards the Midlands, is where we might have a small chance of reaching 36C in one or two spots.

Article continues below

“But Thursday at this stage looks the most likely hottest day of the week. So 36C is a fairly reasonable probability locally on Thursday and there’s a small chance it could get even higher than that.”

News.title: Three men, aged 17, 21 and 23, dead in horror Rotherham crash as police issue plea
News.content:
Three men, aged 17, 21 and 23, dead in horror Rotherham crash as police issue plea

A 17-year-old boy and two men, aged 21 and 23, have been killed following a serious collision which saw a vehicle leave a carriageway on rural country lane in Rotherham

View Image South Yorkshire Police are at the scene (Image: PA)

Two men and a teenager have been killed in a horror collision on a rural country lane in South Yorkshire.

‌



Police were called to reports of a crash involving one car on Denaby Lane in Rotherham at 11.39pm on Saturday, August 8.

‌



The vehicle, a grey Seat Cupra Leon, was travelling towards Kilnhurst before it left the carriageway, officers said.

‌



Despite the best efforts of emergency services, a 17-year-old boy and two men, aged 21 and 23, were tragically pronounced dead at the scene.

Another teenage boy, aged 17, was taken to hospital with minor injuries.

‌



The victim's families have been informed and are being supported by officers, reports Yorkshire Live.

South Yorkshire Police are now asking for anyone who witnessed the collision, or who may have dash cam footage that caught the crash, to contact them.

A police spokesman said: "An investigation is underway and we are now asking for anyone who witnessed the collision, or who may have dash cam footage that could assist with our enquiries, to come forward.

Article continues below

"If you can help, please report online or call 101, quoting incident number 1235 of 8 August 2026.

"People who witnessed the crash can report information through the SYP online portal here here. Footage can be submitted here.

Information can be reported anonymously via the independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111 or on the Crimestoppers website.

News.title: Nigel Farage watch live: Reform chief unveils plan to remove foreign nationals from UK prisons to El Salvador jails
News.content:
Nigel Farage will take questions from the press at an event today

Nigel Farage has announced a new headline-grabbing policy on prisons - and will hope it goes better than Reform's efforts on small boats and illegal working last week

Nigel Farage is desperately hoping to unveil a new policy that doesn't instantly fall apart after a disastrous week.

The under-fire Reform UK leader, whose party has dropped behind Labour in several polls, is holding a press conference now. He announced plans to send foreign criminals to jails overseas.

It comes after France torpedoed his thin small boats plan a week ago, and home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf was branded a "pillock" after announcing an illegal working policy that Labour has already done.

Mr Farage was accused of unveiling headline-grabbing ideas to distract from sleaze allegations. On Thursday he faces a humiliating face-off with Count Binface in an ill-thought-through by-election in Clacton.

He is the overwhelming favourite to win, but if he returns to Parliament a probe into an undeclared £5million gift he received from crypto tycoon Christopher Harborne is expected to resume. If he is found to have broken rules for MPs, it could trigger a second by-election.

Follow live updates below...

News.title: Co-operative Bank gives 'one-week' alert as millions eligible for extra £100 payment
News.content:
Co-operative Bank gives 'one-week' alert as millions eligible for extra £100 payment

It makes for a total of £300 in free cash

View 3 Images The Co-operative Bank has a deal on (Image: The Co-Operative Bank)

The Co-operative Bank is reminding customers that there is now just a week left to bag an extra £100 payment, giving those eligible a total of £300.

‌



It said time was ticking to take advantage of what is called "its biggest-ever switching offer", with eligible customers able to receive up to £300 when they switch their current account. The bank said that customers switching to either a Standard Current Account or Everyday Extra could receive up to £200 - £125 upfront and £25 per month for three months when actively using the account.

‌



In addition, eligible Co-operative Bank and Coventry Building Society customers could receive a further £100 loyalty bonus, but this element of the offer closes on August 17, 2026.

‌



More than four million customers are eligible for the additional £100 payment, which it claimed made it one of the most generous switching incentives currently available on the market. The switch offer comes alongside a range of recent changes to the Bank’s Everyday Extra account.

View 3 Images Some customers get an extra £100 (Image: Nigel Harris via Getty Images)

The refreshed package now costs £12 per month, reduced from £18, and provides benefits worth more than £640, the bank said. Travel and mobile phone insurance covers everyone in the household. UK and European breakdown cover can also be used when travelling as a passenger in someone else’s car.

‌



The bank said it had already removed its 2.75% foreign transaction fee on debit card spending overseas – now a standard feature across all of its current accounts. Current account holders will also have access to the Regular Saver account, offering an exclusive 7.00% gross/AER variable. Customers can open with as little as £1 and save up to £250 each month, earning up to £114 in interest over the 12-month term.

Kat Robinson, head of family and everyday banking at The Co-operative Bank, said: "There is now just a short time left for eligible customers to secure our additional £100 loyalty bonus, so we'd encourage anyone thinking about switching to act before the August 17 deadline.

View 3 Images Free cash deals are a common incentive to switch accounts (Image: Oscar Wong via Getty Images)

Article continues below

"Combined with our £200 switch offer, our loyal customers could receive up to £300, while also benefiting from improvements we've made across our current account range, including fee-free debit card spending overseas and access to our competitive Regular Saver account.

"For customers looking for even more value, our Everyday Extra account now costs £12 a month and includes a range of insurance and protection benefits designed to support people at home and when travelling abroad."

"The additional £100 payment has been a great way for us to recognise the loyalty of Co-operative Bank and Coventry Building Society customers, and we're pleased to be giving people one final opportunity to take advantage of it before the offer ends."

News.title: How to make a safe DIY viewer for Wednesday's historic 2026 UK solar eclipse
News.content:
How to make a safe DIY viewer for Wednesday's historic 2026 UK solar eclipse

As families up and down the country prepare for a rare partial solar eclipse, a DIY pinhole projector should help captivate pint-sized astronomers

How to watch the solar eclipse

This week, stargazers young and old are in for a real celestial treat: the most significant solar eclipse to hit our skies since 1999.

‌



On the evening of Wednesday, August 12, shortly after 6 pm, the Moon will pass directly between the Earth and the Sun, covering roughly nine-tenths of the solar face. A narrow path across Greenland, Iceland, and Northern Spain will experience a total eclipse, plunging the landscape into daytime darkness.

‌



Across the UK and Ireland, spectators can look forward to an impressive partial solar eclipse, with stronger coverage in the south-west regions reaching as much as 96 percent - a real historic feat. For many of us, this marks the last occasion in our lifetimes when we can expect to see an eclipse of such near totality on our shores.

‌



Exact times Solar Eclipse 2026 will take place across UK - every area listed READ MORE :

12 View 12 Images You'll need scissors, tape, tinfoil, white card, a pin, and a pinch of creativity 12 View 12 Images First of all, take one piece of card and fold it in half, so that there's a crease down the middle

It will be another 55 years before a partial eclipse of this magnitude returns, while a total solar eclipse won't be visible from the UK until 2090.

While this is an event you won't want to miss, enthusiastic observers should be mindful that it's never safe to stare into the sun, and that this can cause permanent retinal damage.

‌



Unless you have genuine eclipse glasses (which have widely sold out), viewing the eclipse indirectly with your back to the Sun is the safest way to enjoy this rare occurrence in all its glory.

Fortunately, you don't need expensive astronomical gear to experience the magic, making this a perfect summer holiday craft project for young space enthusiasts.

12 View 12 Images Cut a square in the centre of your first piece of paper, just over where the crease is 12 View 12 Images Snip yourself a square piece of tinfoil

‌



What you'll need:

Two sheets of white card

Scissors

Sticky tape

Aluminium foil

A pushpin

How to make your projector:

How to make and use your projector:

Cut the window: Fold one sheet of white card in half, then cut a small square out along the fold line. Unfold it to reveal a small central window.

‌



View 12 Images Place your tinfoil square over your paper 'window', covering it

Attach the foil: Cut a piece of foil slightly larger than the square, lay it over the window, and tape it down tightly on all four sides. Make the pinhole: Gently pierce a single hole through the centre of the foil with your pin. (Adult supervision is recommended for little hands!)

View 12 Images Then, fasten your tinfoil in place using a bit of tape

‌



Project the image: Stand with your back to the Sun. Hold the card with the foil window so sunlight hits it directly, placing the second blank sheet of card behind it as a screen. The light passing through the pinhole will project a tiny, sharp disc of the Sun onto your screen.

View 12 Images Jab a hole through the centre of the tinfoil square, creating a small hole

‌



With your simple yet nifty projector in place, it's time to wait for the extraordinary moment when the moon blots out the sun, and in turn, your miniature disc.

View 12 Images Once in the correct position, the sun will shine through the tiny hole, creating a disc

What to expect and where to look:

The solar eclipse begins with 'first contact', as the Moon begins moving across the Sun.

‌



After reaching its maximum point, it will then gradually come to an end as the moon drifts onwards and away.

While there won't be complete darkness in the UK, the light will dip noticeably. Exact timings will differ depending on where in the UK you are. Maximum eclipse will occur between 7.05 pm and 7.16 pm, approximately.

12 View 12 Images You can replicate this using a cheesegrater 12 View 12 Images Or even a colander

‌



Should you want to practice this beforehand with curious youngsters, then grab yourself a bit of black card as your 'moon', passing over the top of the hole to mimic that awe-inspiring moment.

For those with less time on their plate for arts and crafts this week, the same effect can be achieved with your everyday cheese grater or colander.

Do make sure to still use a blank piece of white card or paper for your projector screen, however. This makes for a much clearer image, not to mention more wonder for your budding astronomers.

‌



12 View 12 Images It's essential that you use a white piece of card or paper as a projector screen 12 View 12 Images There's no need to invest in fancy equipment ahead of the eclipse

While some parts of the country will be graced with more coverage, there are a few things you can do to ensure that your family's solar eclipse night is a true out-of-this-world experience.

‌



The Royal Astronomical Society advises avoiding artificial light and built-up areas if at all possible, to allow for greater immersion. Meanwhile, Skyscanner notes that the sun will already be quite low by the time of the maximum eclipse, and could well end up obscured by buildings, trees or hills.

Astronomy enthusiasts are therefore encouraged to seek viewing points which look out uninterrupted towards either the west or west-north-west. "Open or elevated ground without nearby buildings and trees" would be ideal here, especially with "enough space to avoid blocking paths or crowding narrow viewpoints".

Whether you're watching from the breathtaking Outer Hebrides or a city garden in London, the 2026 solar eclipse looks set to be one to remember.

News.title: Chessington World of Adventures forced to close in middle of summer holidays
News.content:
Chessington World of Adventures forced to close in middle of summer holidays

Chessington World of Adventures will be closed today with no information yet available about when the London theme park will reopen

View 2 Images It is unclear when the park will reopen

A popular theme park in London has been forced to close following a water outage.

‌



Chessington World of Adventures will be closed for the day with park operators apologising for the inconvenience. It is unclear when the park will reopen or what caused the water outage.

‌



Visitors will be able to use their tickets booked for today on other days.

‌



A spokesperson from Chessington World of Adventures said: "We are currently experiencing operational disruption due to a burst water main that is affecting the local area.

"As a result, the attraction is closed today while our teams work closely with Thames Water and local partners to restore normal operations as quickly and safely as possible.

View 2 Images Visitors being informed about the closure by a staff member at Chessington World of Adventures this morning (Image: Zoe Linkson/PA Wire)

‌



"We appreciate the patience and understanding of our guests and can confirm that anyone impacted will be automatically revalidated under our Return Promise. The safety of our guests and employees remains our highest priority."

Thames Water reported at around 11.15am that a burst was affecting customers in the KT9 area, which covers Chessington World of Adventures. People in the area are experiencing low or no water pressure as a result.

Thames Water said: "We’re sorry if your tap water isn’t running at the moment. We’re aware of a burst that's affecting customers in the KT9 area.

‌



"Our specialist team is on site and have located a burst water main on Leatherhead Road. We are working to carry out the repair on the damaged pipe to get water flowing through your taps as soon as possible.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

"We know how disruptive it is if you lose your water supply, so we’ll work hard to get things back to normal as soon as we can." A hosepipe ban has been in place for Thames Water customers since July 23.

‌



Crowds have been pictured at the park following the closure announcement, which reportedly took place shortly after the opening at 10am.

This left many customers frustrated, as the Sun reports one dad called the situation "utter shambles", with another adding they had spent "hundreds on an overnight stay and fast passes".

Chessington World of Adventures have enacted their "return promise", which allows customers who have pre-booked tickets to return for free within nine months of their visit on selected dates. Chessington, which is owned by Merlin Entertainments, has not specified which dates will be open for a free return visit, but the school holiday period typically ends at the start of September.

Article continues below

Chessington World of Adventures welcomes up to 1.75million visitors every year, making it one of the top-visited theme parks in the UK and Europe.

News.title: Mount Etna eruption - what to do you if you have an Italy holiday booked
News.content:
Mount Etna eruption - what to do you if you have an Italy holiday booked

Flights to Italy's fifth busiest airport have been suspended and advice has been issued for any Brits who are due to fly to the Mediterranean island in the next few days

View 2 Images Volcanic activity that has caused airborne ash has forced flight cancellations (Image: Salvatore Allegra/Anadolu via Getty Images)

An eruption at Europe's largest and tallest active volcano has led to the closure of one of Italy's busiest airports, throwing travel plans into chaos for many Brits.

‌



Mount Etna is one of the world's most active volcanoes, and over the weekend it was spotted bellowing smoke and ashes into the atmosphere, forcing the suspension of arrivals into nearby Catania-Fontanarossa Airport.

‌



In a statement posted today on its official website, airport officials said: "Due to Etna’s eruptive activity and the associated release of volcanic ash into the atmosphere, the airspace corresponding to the ash cloud southwest of the volcano (Sector C1) has been closed. Arrivals are suspended until 5:00 PM.

‌



"As the situation is significantly affecting operations, passengers are kindly advised to check the status of their flight with their airline before heading to the airport. The situation is being constantly monitored, and further updates will be provided depending on the evolution of volcanic activity and weather conditions."

View 2 Images Mount Etna also erupted last month leading to a two-day shutdown of the local airport (Image: Giuseppe Distefano / Etna Walk / AFP via Getty Images)

Initially, the airport allowed a small number of landings until the early hours of this morning, before the decision was made to suspend flights completely. Other airports on the island are currently unaffected.

‌



Airlines with routes from the UK to Catania include British Airways, easyJet, Jet2, Ryanair, and Wizz Air, and passengers who have a flight booked to the airport should immediately check their flight status on its official website. Passengers may see flight delays, diversions, or cancellations to their itineraries, and airlines should be getting in touch with any holidaymakers affected by the change.

Volcanic activity on Mount Etna has often affected flights to Catania, due to its location just 29 miles from the volcano, and passengers are sometimes re-routed to other Sicilian airports such as Palermo. Similar cancellations and diversions were seen at Catania just last month, with a two-day closure on July 5 and 6.

It's worth noting that at the moment, the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) doesn't have any warnings in place about visiting the island, it simply advises "Check with your travel provider or Catania airport before travelling." Other than any exclusion zones close to the volcano, Brits are still free to visit the island, but should look out for local emergency updates.

‌



Exact date Brits could face fresh wave of airport chaos as new rule kicks in READ MORE :

Flight cancelled and passengers stranded due to child's actions READ MORE :

While flight delays of over three hours often allow passengers to claim for compensation, a volcanic eruption usually comes under 'extraordinary circumstances', which means a claim is unlikely to be successful.

However, passengers from the UK to Sicily are still covered by the Denied Boarding Regulation, also known as EU Regulation 261/2004, meaning airlines need to assist them during delays. For a flight to Sicily, this would come into force for any delay over three hours.

Airlines need to provide two free phone calls or emails to each passenger, meals and refreshments that are appropriate to the time of day and delay length - usually given as vouchers - and hotel transfers and accommodation if the delay is overnight.

News.title: Record 230 people cross Channel in one small boat
News.content:
A small boat has crossed the English Channel carrying 230 people, the largest number to make the journey in a single vessel.

It breaks the previous record set in July, when 165 people made the crossing on a single vessel.

The boat arrived in the UK in the early hours of Monday.

A picture taken off the coast of northern France showed the inflatable boat was so full many passengers had to dangle their legs in the water as it entered the busy shipping route.

A Home Office spokesperson said this latest incident demonstrated the "reckless and dangerous tactics employed by criminal gangs... who continue to put lives at risk by cramming ever greater numbers of people onto unseaworthy vessels".

French rescuers said the 15m (49ft) boat was "buckling" in the water and could have led to a "tragedy".

The boat was already carrying about 50 people when it was seen heading towards a beach to pick more passengers up, the crew in Berck-sur-Mer added.

The SNMS team, the equivalent of the UK's RNLI, said about 30 people ended up in the water during the rush to climb onboard.

Part of the group also became cut off by the tide and had to be rescued, a translated statement said.

News.title: 'Dust devil' spins through London park
News.content:
Footage captured on Sunday in Greenwich Park, south-east London, showed a small whirlwind, or dust devil, swirling around people.

Jimmy O'Keeffe - who took the footage - says he was "shocked and in total disbelief" as his picnic was disturbed.

Dust devils are formed on warm, sunny days and are visible due to the dust or hay that they pick up and swirl around.

The weather phenomenon was also seen north-east of Leeds Castle in Kent this weekend.

In Greenwich, some people got up from their picnics as the "dust devil" moved across the park, with some even heard screaming.

O'Keeffe - who's 35 and originally from Manchester, although lives in Greenwich - says it lasted for a few minutes before disappearing.

He adds that most people stayed calm - and that his picnic food had a "lucky escape".

Reporting by Maddie Lake

More on England weather.

News.title: Travelodge staff gave domestic abuser key to his victim's room
News.content:
Another woman, Jo from Leeds, contacted BBC News following coverage of the Maidenhead attack.

In July, she woke in her room to an unknown man standing at the end of her bed, and screamed for help.

"It was just horrible, it was horrendous. Terrifying. I was shaking so badly," she said.

Her friend who was staying in the room heard him say, "I'm sorry, they gave me this key," she said.

Jo considered staying elsewhere following the reports of the attack in 2022, but was reassured by Travelodge's chief executive Jo Boydell, who previously said: "The safety and security of customers in our hotels is extremely important and we want everyone to be safe, and feel safe, in our hotels."

Jo said: "What happened to us shouldn't have happened. And the assurances [Travelodge] gave are not accurate. The systems are failing."

In response, Travelodge said an investigation found "our updated room access security policies, which were in place at the time, were not correctly followed, which is not acceptable.

"We have retrained the hotel team on our current room security and check-in procedures."

Andy Smith, who has travelled the country with his band and stays in dozens of Travelodge hotels a year, said he had been given keys to other people's rooms recently.

"We went up to the room and there was a guy already asleep in there in a state of undress," he said.

It followed another incident about 18 months ago where another man had gained access to his room by telling reception staff he was checking in under a common name such as "Mr Smith", Andy Smith said.

"I think he just chanced it. Because my name's Smith, I think it's just the pure luck of it. I mean, why wouldn't anyone be asking for ID or anything, like a booking reference or an email address. It beggars belief."

Travelodge responded by saying "any case of an unauthorised person entering a guest's room is a significant cause for concern and we want to be clear that these incidents should not have happened".

News.title: Thames Water gave finance boss a £1m signing-on fee
News.content:
Thames Water paid its finance chief a Â£1m signing-on fee in July as the company struggles with a mountain of debt and faces temporary nationalisation.

Steve Buck joined the company in April 2025 but it is understood the seven-figure payment was not made until last month after the company had taken legal advice over its contractual obligations.

The existence of the payment, first reported by Sky News,, external was revealed in a letter from the Thames Water chairman to MPs on the Commons Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee.

In the letter,, external Sir Adrian Montague said he understood customers would see large payments to senior leaders as "unjust" but argued they were necessary to stop staff leaving.

The letter said: "The majority of the team were brought in recently to fix the problems the company faces and are not responsible for causing those problems.

"These talented and experienced individuals have opportunities for roles outside Thames Water and, in many cases, have been actively approached by other companies.

"These roles would be less in the public gaze, less difficult and more remunerative."

Sir Adrian described the payment to Buck as a "necessary incentive" and said the money had come from emergency funding provided by Thames Water's lenders.

He said the company is facing recruitment and retention difficulties and warned the problem would "persist" if it was nationalised or put into special administration.

Alistair Carmichael, Lib Dem MP and chair of the Environment Committee, said: "Money should be going into improving services, not remunerating already well-paid senior executives.

"The government were clear in the early days that they wanted this to stop. It is obvious that they have not succeeded in this. We need to hear now from them about what they intend to do about it."

The utility company owes roughly Â£20bn and has been working with creditors and government officials to find a way forward.

Failure to reach a deal could lead to Thames Water being forced into a "special administration regime", a form of temporary nationalisation intended to keep the business operating until a viable solution can be found.

This would see government-appointed officials temporarily running the company â including funding its operations and upgrading infrastructure as well as dealing with any outstanding debts following a restructuring of the business.

If the company was subsequently sold to a private buyer, the government would be able to recoup some taxpayer cash.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has previously said he would like to see "greater public control" of key water and energy utilities.

In the past year, Thames Water boss Chris Weston saw his pay increase 14% to Â£1.63m while other directors received bonuses totalling Â£4.1m.

Speaking on the BBC Big Boss interview late last month, Weston acknowledged there was anger about Thames Water pay, but argued that the company needed to be able attract "capable people to help turn this company around".

"If we're not prepared to pay market rates, then they won't come to us and they won't stay with us," he said.

News.title: Ex-Cambridge professor Jason Arday cancels live event after plagiarism row
News.content:
Jason Arday has cancelled an appearance in London next month, following his resignation as a Cambridge professor in the wake of allegations of plagiarism and questions about some of his achievements.

Arday's talk at the Royal Geographical Society's conference has been "cancelled at the request of the speaker", the organisation said.

He is also no longer listed on the websites of two other scheduled events in the coming months.

Arday - who became Cambridge's youngest ever black professor in 2023 - has admitted errors in his early work, but said he was not a "liar" and that the recent furore had led to "an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack".

He had been due to take part in a "fireside chat" at the Royal Geographical Society's conference in London on 2 September.

Arday's appearance at Topping & Company book shop in Edinburgh on 18 September is no longer listed on the website and has reportedly also been cancelled. The shop declined to comment.

He was also announced as a guest for the Arizona Women's Board Authors' Luncheon on 24 October, but is no longer listed on the event's website.

He is still listed as a speaker for the Stroud Book Festival in Gloucestershire in November.

News.title: Asylum seeker who groomed and raped girl, 13, jailed
News.content:
An asylum seeker who raped a 13-year-old girl after pretending to be a teenager on Snapchat has been jailed.

Abdul Khan attacked the girl in a nature reserve in Clifton, Nottingham, on 14 May last year.

Khan arrived in the UK in the back of a lorry in 2015, Nottingham Crown Court heard, and faces automatic deportation to Afghanistan after he has served two thirds of his sentence.

He was jailed for nine and a half years on Monday after he was convicted of two counts of rape, one count of sexual activity with a child, sexual communication with a child, meeting a child following grooming and perverting the course of justice.

A four-day trial was told Khan, who is believed to be 28 and already serving a 23-month sentence for sexual communication with a different child in Derbyshire, arranged to meet his victim in woodland after telling her on the Snapchat messaging app he was a 14-year-old boy.

When they met in person and it was clear he was not 14, he tried to appease her by claiming to be 16, the court heard.

After activity that jurors found had been consensual, Khan, of HMP Nottingham, twice raped the girl.

Judge Mark Watson said the victim told her father what had happened and he contacted police.

Khan was then linked to the rapes by a mobile phone seized during his arrest over his contact with the child in Derbyshire.

Yet despite DNA evidence subsequently linking him to the attack, Nottinghamshire Police said he continued to deny having met the victim.

Addressing Khan, the judge said: "You deliberately concealed your true identity. She thought she was communicating with a child of her own age.

"It was a lie you have persisted with throughout these proceedings."

News.title: Nigel Farage says incident at his home 'directly linked' to Ann Widdecombe murder
News.content:
Nigel Farage said an incident at his London home last year was "directly linked" to the murder of Ann Widdecombe, after counter-terror police reopened an inquiry into it last week.

It relates to what Farage described as a "lit incendiary device" being pushed through his letterbox in April 2025, the BBC understands.

Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) London has also referred itself to the police watchdog over how the initial investigation was handled.

At a Monday press conference, the Reform UK leader said: "I understand this is a completely unprecedented move, and yes, this is directly linked to the murder of Ann Widdecombe, and I'm afraid I just can't tell you any more than that at this stage."

News.title: British couple held in Iran end hunger strike
News.content:
A British couple jailed in Iran after being accused of espionage have ended their hunger strikes after 93 and 84 days respectively.

Craig and Lindsay Foreman were arrested in January 2025 while passing through Iran on a motorcycle journey from Europe to Australia. They were both sentenced to 10 years in jail in February, but Craig Foreman's family said his punishment had been extended by two years after speaking to the media.

The couple from East Sussex, who both deny espionage, went on hunger strike in May when prison authorities prevented them from calling their families.

The family of the couple said they had been protesting against how they and other prisoners were being treated.

A spokesperson for the family said the couple agreed with prison guards to end their strike to be able to speak directly to their loved ones again.

However, the family said contact was yet to be re-established, as of Monday afternoon.

The family had also previously called for the couple to end their hunger strike.

Five people outside the prison joined the pair on their hunger strike for the final five days as an act of solidarity, the family added.

The fast ran from Tuesday to Saturday with Lindsay Foreman's son Joe Bennett and four unnamed others taking part in the UK, as well as other prisoners inside Tehran's Evin jail, the family said.

"My mum and Craig have spent months on hunger strike, and even at the point of bringing it to an end they wanted to make it about something bigger than themselves," Bennett, from Folkestone in Kent, said.

"Those final five days became about people standing together around values that should be universal: Truth, justice, kindness, peace and unity."

By the end of the protest, Craig Foreman had been on hunger strike for 93 days, and Lindsay Foreman for 84 days, the family added.

Although they said they were unaware of the condition of the pair, who had consumed just milk and either honey or salt in water during their strikes.

Bennett said the couple also went on a seperate hunger striker back in November as a "cry out for help".

News.title: Ban on 'subscription traps' brought forward by three months
News.content:
Subscriptions will be easier to cancel and companies will be compelled to make it clear when contracts auto-renew at a higher price, Andy Burnham has announced.

The prime minister is also planning to outlaw shops from falsely claiming products previously retailed at much higher prices to advertise supposed deals, which he said tricks shoppers into thinking they are getting better value on purchases.

Burnham will bring forward a package of changes announced under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer to end so-called subscription traps and a crackdown on "pretend prices".

Shadow chancellor Mel Stride branded the measures "reheated" and said the prime minister "has already run out of ideas".

The plans were announced under Sir Keir in April, but are being brought forward by Burnham's government in a bid to give families "room to breathe" amid the high cost of living.

On subscriptions, the government said the changes will mean businesses have "to provide clearer up-front information, regular reminders and a much easier exit to contracts" for customers.

Burnham, who is embarking on a tour of the UK while Parliament is in recess, has promised a series of "everyday fixes" to help people with the cost of living.

He said: "I'm determined to pull every single lever we can to provide people with some room to breathe on the cost of living."

The measures being brought forward are aimed at making it easier for consumers to cancel unwanted subscriptions and stopping people being rolled onto expensive contracts without their knowledge.

They were expected to come into force next spring, but Burnham's government has promised they will now be implemented by January 2027.

When they were announced in April, the government said the plans would save consumers Â£400m a year in total, or up to Â£170 per person.

At the time, the Department for Business and Trade said there are 10 million unwanted, active subscriptions across the UK.

It said that more than 3.5 million people are being "quietly rolled from free or discounted trials into fully costed contracts", while another 1.3 million are caught out by unexpected auto-renewals.

On top of the already planned changes, Burnham is also vowing to end shops' use of "pretend prices". This will stop retailers using "was" prices, made-up discounts or misleading recommended retail prices (RRPs) to highlight deals.

The government will launch a consultation this autumn to decide how the new measures should be implemented.

News.title: Ex-PE teacher who hit children with golf balls ordered to do unpaid work
News.content:
A former PE teacher has been ordered to carry out 300 hours of unpaid work for violent attacks on teenage pupils at a scandal-hit residential school in North Ayrshire.

Michael Neil, 72, locked children in the gym hall and struck them with golf balls at the now-closed Kerelaw in Stevenston between 1991 and 2003.

The ex-footballer, who played for Arbroath and Clyde, carried out so many attacks on pupils that a jury heard he could not even remember them.

At sentencing, Sheriff Eoin McGinty said Neil's pupils had experienced "fear, humiliation and physical harm" - but he decided against a jail sentence for reasons including Neil's "advanced years".

He is the latest former staff member to be convicted of offences at the school and will be supervised for two years.

In 2024, Police Scotland declared a "critical incident" over the scale of its investigation into historical abuse allegations at Kerelaw.

News.title: Radio Caroline breached Ofcom rules after mistakenly announcing King's death
News.content:
Radio Caroline has been found in breach of broadcasting rules after it mistakenly announced the death of King Charles III.

The station aired three pre-recorded announcements falsely stating the King had died during the Barry Marsh Show on 19 May.

The messages claimed the "news media" had "confirmed" the death, and were followed by the national anthem and 16 minutes of silence on DAB+, while AM listeners heard back-up music. A correction and apology was broadcast 30 minutes later.

The ruling by media watchdog Ofcom stated that once the staff member who accidentally played the files realised what they had done, they stopped playing them, "panicked and left the premises".

Ofcom said the incident breached Rule 5.1, which requires news to be reported with due accuracy, and Rule 5.2, which says significant mistakes must be corrected quickly.

It described the false announcement as a "very significant inaccuracy" on a matter of "very high public interest".

The mistake happened after a staff member carrying out maintenance accessed preârecorded obituary files intended for use in the event of the King's death.

Ofcom said the files were played "out of curiosity", cutting off the presenter's remote stream and putting the announcements on air.

News.title: Mars Bar from 1991 found - and it's 20g bigger than one from today
News.content:
A 35-year-old Mars Bar has been found during a house clearance â and the discovery has gone viral amid claims it highlights the effect of "shrinkflation".

The chocolate bar with a best-before date of 1991 was found during a clear-out of a house in Scunthorpe.

Victoria Gordon, who runs the cleaning service, posted a photo on social media of the 62.5g bar alongside one of today's Mars Bars, which is 40g.

"It was nearly as big as my hand, which was kind of why I noticed it," she said.

News.title: Senior detective under investigation over use of AI
News.content:
A senior detective is being investigated over potential artificial intelligence (AI)-related gross misconduct.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said it had started investigating the officer after they were referred to the watchdog by Derbyshire Police following an "internal review" of their use of AI.

The investigation into the force comes two months after a criminal investigation was launched into another officer accused of using AI systems to "create evidential material in a number of cases".

Derbyshire Police said on Monday it made a voluntary referral to the IOPC on 23 June "regarding an officer's use of artificial intelligence".

The force said the latest investigation was being independently led by the IOPC and it was unable to comment further.

The Financial Times (FT), external reported a person familiar with events said the case involved a detective chief inspector at the force alleged to have used AI to maintain "decision logs".

Senior investigators maintain such logs during investigations to record why they took each step, and they can be disclosed for defence lawyers to scrutinise during court cases, the FT said.

News.title: Man, 18, dies after getting into difficulty in sea
News.content:
A man has died after getting into difficulty in the sea on Sunday, emergency services have confirmed.

Sussex Police said it was called to Camber Sands beach in East Sussex just before 19:00 BST on Sunday evening to reports that three people had got into difficulty.

An 18-year-old man was pulled from the water about 30 minutes later, but despite attempts by paramedics, he was pronounced dead a short time later. Police said his next of kin have been informed.

Two other people - a 16-year-old boy and a 24-year-old man - safely returned to shore, the force added.

News.title: Water outage forces Chessington theme park to close
News.content:
Chessington World of Adventures has been forced to close for the day after what the resort described as a water outage in the local area.

The theme park and zoo in south-west London said tickets booked for Monday 10 August would be returned or could be reused.

It did not say what had caused the outage or when it expected to reopen.

The closure falls in the middle of the school summer holidays, one of the busiest periods for UK theme parks.

Chessington apologised for the inconvenience and thanked visitors for their understanding.

The park shut for a day in July 2018 after a burst water main left homes and businesses in the surrounding area without supply or on low pressure.

News.title: Kidnappers made man film naked ransom videos
News.content:
An ex-soldier who was part of a gang which kidnapped and beat a man before making him film naked ransom videos has been jailed for four years.

Mark Pearce, 53, and others took the victim to a caravan in a field owned by Pearce near Stockton for the hours-long ordeal in April 2024, Teesside Crown Court heard.

The kidnappers had disguised themselves as delivery drivers and bundled the man into a van outside his home, the court heard.

Pearce, from Stockton, had denied wrongdoing but was found guilty of conspiracy to kidnap along with Donald Hammond, 43 from London, who was jailed for six years at an earlier hearing.

The victim was confronted by three men in high-vis jackets outside his home and shoved into the back of a van on 13 April 2024, prosecutor Oliver Connor said.

The men were wearing their jackets to make them look like delivery drivers, the court heard.

The victim was taken to a caravan in a field where he was bound with tape and cable ties and blindfolded.

President Donald Trump posted a touched-up photograph of himself from his weekend golf trip, where he appeared much more youthful, instead of sharing the original image.

The 80-year-old president was pictured Sunday at his Bedminster club in New Jersey driving the golf cart alongside retired professional Gary Player, 90, as they attended the LIV Golf New York tournament.

Trump, who often posts about how young he feels for his age, did not share the original photograph on Truth Social but posted a version in which he appeared to have undergone a computer-generated glow-up.

“With the great Gary Player, today, at Bedminster!” the post said.Player, by comparison, appeared almost exactly the same in the computer-generated image as the original.

Some of the president’s critics shared the two images side by side on social media.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump posted a touched-up photograph of himself from his weekend golf trip, along with Gary Player, where he appeared much younger, instead of sharing the original image ( Icon Sportswire/Getty )

open image in gallery Trump appeared to have undergone an glow-up, while Player appeared essentially the same as he did in the original image ( @realDonaldTrump )

“Trump’s AI Image vs. Reality,” quipped the anti-Trump Patriot Takes account.

“First image: Trump posted it bragging about playing golf this weekend. Second image: Actual photograph of 2 elderly men pretending to play golf this weekend,” said Brian Krassenstein, a liberal influencer and frequent critic of Trump’s.

Natalie Harp, Trump’s longtime devoted aide, is reportedly the person helping the president with his Truth Social posts, and compiles screenshots of social media posts from allies or fans praising the president for him to review. Harp was pictured returning to the White House with the president this weekend.

The Independent has contacted the White House for comment.

Trump was also pictured over the weekend with markings on his right arm. The discoloration on the president’s hands has become a subject of persistent scrutiny, but the apparently new markings on his arm prompted fresh speculation.

The White House has repeatedly brushed off concerns, attributing the marks to the physical toll of Trump’s constant public engagement.

open image in gallery Trump was also pictured over the weekend with markings on his right arm ( Reuters )

“President Trump is the sharpest, most accessible, and energetic president in American history,” White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said previously in a statement provided to The Independent. “The President is a man of the people and he meets more Americans and shakes their hands on a daily basis than any other President in history.”

Trump’s appearance came under further scrutiny last week after pictures of the president’s new hairdo went viral.

The commander-in-chief sported a seemingly brighter and fuller head of hair as he gave a speech in Las Vegas, prompting his estranged niece, Mary Trump, to liken him to Hermey the Elf from the animated Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer.

“I’m not going to say anything about whether it looked good or not. I don't really care,” she told SiriusXM host Dean Obeidallah’s YouTube show. “However, he looked like Herby the Dentist from ‘Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer’ — that’s what, that was my takeaway.”

Urging shoppers to repair worn garments rather than buy new ones might seem like a counterproductive retail strategy. However, offering in-store repairs and sewing workshops has become an essential service for clothing brands seeking to appeal to young consumers focused on saving money and protecting the planet.

While high-end fashion houses and outdoor retailers like Patagonia and L.L. Bean have offered product repairs for decades, the concept is gaining wider traction. Mainstream apparel chains, including Levi Strauss & Co., Uniqlo, and budget retailer Primark, are among the companies hoping to win over Generation Z buyers with a needle and thread.

Levi's created a handstitching course for high school students after identifying that many Gen Z consumers lacked basic sewing skills despite their interest in thrifting and sustainability. Staff members spend 90 minutes teaching teenagers four basic tasks: sewing on a button, hemming, patching a hole, and fixing a tear.

The Wear Longer program, which the San Francisco-based company is expanding across the U.S., builds upon the mending and customization services Levi's provides at hundreds of locations globally.

open image in gallery Jesse Sanchez practices sewing during a clothing repair workshop at a Levi's retail store in downtown San Francisco in July 2026 ( AP Photo/Terry Chea )

"We think it’s important to empower the people who buy our clothes with the skill sets to maintain them, to get them to that second life," Paul Dillinger, Levi's head of global design innovation, said.

Detroit resident Chloe Halprin, 25, represents the type of consumer retailers aim to reach with a message centered on repairing rather than discarding clothes.

In high school, Halprin routinely bought cheap, trend-focused items. Fixing a major rip was beyond her limited sewing ability, meaning damaged tops or skirts from Forever 21 were often discarded: "I might just throw it away."

Today, Halprin, a nonprofit grant writer, purchases most of her clothing secondhand. Having recently learned to hem on a sewing machine, she plans to attempt projects like turning a skirt into a shirt.

"I try to be conscientious of my carbon footprint," Halprin said. "I really don’t like waste. I’m trying to save money as well."

Mending is a tiny part of cutting the world's mountains of textile waste

Mending remains a small component of addressing global textile waste, but its shift from a craft to a customer retention tool comes amid rising pressure on the fashion industry to reduce pollution and climate impacts.

Textile waste—including manufacturing scraps, unwanted clothing and linens, and unsold goods—is a major industry hurdle. The United Nations Environment Program estimates global fabric waste is generated at a rate equivalent to a garbage truck being dumped or incinerated every second.

Researchers agree that repairing and reselling clothing reduces environmental impact, particularly if it replaces a new purchase. However, many warn these practices remain too limited to offset ongoing growth in garment manufacturing and consumption.

open image in gallery Levi’s employees teach students during a sewing workshop at a Levi's retail store in downtown San Francisco ( AP Photo/Terry Chea )

Global clothing production roughly doubled from 2000 to 2015, while the average number of wearings per garment dropped by about 36%, according to the Ellen MacArthur Foundation. The sustainability nonprofit estimated that less than 1% of discarded clothing materials were recycled into new apparel.

Generation Z, born between 1997 and 2012, grew up with fast fashion and e-commerce before facing the economic effects of the coronavirus pandemic and post-pandemic inflation.

Whether driven by tighter budgets or an aversion to materialism, Gen Z has fueled faster growth in the preowned apparel market than in traditional U.S. retail sales, market intelligence firm GlobalData estimated in a report with resale platform ThredUp.

For companies producing new clothing, repair initiatives address "some deeper consumer needs and consumer behaviors at the moment," GlobalData retail analyst Neil Saunders said.

"It puts a halo on the brand," he said.

Skeptics say the environmental impact of retailer repairs is limited

The hands-on response from mass-market retailers, especially fast-fashion chains like Primark, Zara and H&M, has generated interest as well as skepticism.

Zara, which has its headquarters in Spain, launched a digital platform in 2022 for customers to resell their used pieces and to request basic alterations and repairs. The program is available in 17 of the nearly 100 countries where the trend-driven retailer operates.

Ireland-based Primark has focused more on customer education. The value-focused retailer hosts free “Love It For Longer” events where customers are taught skills like replacing zippers and buttons.

“Learning how to repair and care for clothing is probably one of the most simplest but absolutely totally effective ways that we can reduce waste and also extend the lifetime of whatever we buy,” Vicki Swain, Primark’s product longevity & partnership lead, said.

The company has held the workshops — more than 730 altogether — in nine of the 17 countries where Primark has stores, including the U.S. Primark also tested in-store repairs at three U.K. locations this year.

Swain argues that affordable clothes can be just as durable and repair-worthy as more expensive ones. Half the items Primark sells annually are basics like socks, underwear, T-shirts, and jeans, she said.

open image in gallery Whether driven by tighter budgets or an aversion to materialism, Gen Z has fueled faster growth in the preowned apparel market than in traditional U.S. retail sales ( AP Photo/Terry Chea )

“There is nothing throw away about our products,” Swain said.

Uniqlo, which focuses on timeless wardrobe staples, offers a range of aftercare services, including repairs, decorative sashiko mending, embroidery and creative restyling.

Available in 75 of the Japanese mass-market retailer’s roughly 2,500 stores worldwide, the services are promoted as a national extension of the product life cycle. Providing them also strengthens Uniqlo’s connection with customers, said Jean-Emmanuel Shein, director of global corporate responsibility at Uniqlo USA.

Kate Fletcher, a professor of sustainability, design and fashion systems at Manchester Metropolitan University in England, said she thinks the repair initiatives of popular retailers are well-meaning, but she doubts they will have much environmental impact.

“The fashion sector’s primary source of impact is due to the overproduction of pieces and growing volumes of garments created,” Fletcher said. “Repairing a garment in store happens in addition to these growing production volumes, not instead of them.”

Companies want tax incentives to make repairs and secondhand sales more profitable

The question facing the fashion industry is whether repairs can evolve from niche service to commercially viable.

Sweden's H&M Group, which has more than 4,000 stores in over 80 countries, has been unusually candid about one of the biggest obstacles: the economics. The company has argued that repair and resale are desirable goals, but manufacturing new garments costs businesses less than keeping existing ones in use.

H&M experimented with mending and redesign studios in several European flagship stores over the past decade. The company also is majority owner of a secondhand clothing platform called Sellpy.

In May, H&M joined Primark, ThredUp and dozens of other fashion and textile businesses in signing a statement that urged governments in North America and the European Union to adopt tax policies that would make repairing and reselling clothes profitable.

Making mending work in retail is challenging because it's labor intensive and must be priced low enough to entice customers, Saunders, of GlobalData, said. Signals from consumers also are mixed, he said.

“I think younger shoppers still shop fast fashion because even though it goes against some of their principles, it is one of the most accessible parts of the market," Saunders said. "But what they’re doing as well, though, is they’re buying into alternative channels like resale. And they’re having things repaired.”

A British defence firm founded only two years ago has attained a valuation of £2.5bn ($3.4bn), following a funding round which makes it one of the most valuable startups in the UK.

Cambridge Aerospace develops and makes interceptor systems for use against drones and missiles, as well as a radar system and rocket motors.

Defence secretary Wes Streeting called the multi-billion valuation “a great vote of confidence” in Britain that would continue to put the UK “at the forefront of defence innovation”.

The most recent funding round for Cambridge was only in April of this year - the current one marks an increase in overall valuation of well over double since then.

Part of the reason for the rapid increase has been a series of Ministry of Defence contracts earned by Cambridge Aerospace, providing their interceptors for the UK Armed Forces.

The company employs more than 250 workers it describes as highly skilled or in engineering roles, while outside of Britain it operates in other European nations including Germany and Ukraine, as well as Australia.

Seb Johnson, tech business writer and founder of Scaling Europe, noted Cambridge Aerospace is one of three UK-based defence firms to have hit unicorn status - valuations of $1bn or more - in 2026, with the UK having previously had zero. Uforce and Kraken Technology Group are the others.

In May of this year, the government - then under Keir Starmer - signed deals to provide contracts worth up to £4m to 13 different businesses to work with the MoD, as part of a wider scheme to help startups and SMEs progress to unicorn status and aid wider economic growth in key industries.

Cambridge Aerospace was not listed as one of the firms awarded contracts on that occasion.

( Cambridge Aerospace )

Professor Steven Barrett, an aerospace engineer, is the chief executive of the firm. “By bringing together the best talent in the world with a singular mission to protect Allied skies from threats we have achieved a huge amount already,” he said. “The addition of these funds will allow us to continue to scale our manufacturing and our delivery to meet the pace of threats, and the needs of Allied nations.”

Grant Shapps was formerly the chair of the firm but stepped down in June having breached rules on ex-ministers’ business appointments. Mr Barrett says Cambridge have “no plans to appoint anyone new” as a replacement and that Mr Shapps’ “role was only ever titular in nature”.

Mr Streeting added: “This valuation is a great vote of confidence in Britain. Cambridge Aerospace’s Skyhammer is an example of the low-cost interceptor missiles our Armed Forces need to deter adversaries and keep our country safe.

“It is exactly what our unicorn scheme is designed to create – British start-ups scaling into billion-pound companies, creating skilled jobs, cementing the UK’s position at the forefront of defence innovation.”

Solar eclipses glasses are almost impossible to buy in-store and online – and members of the public have been issued with an urgent warning over trying other techniques.

On the high street and internet stores, eclipses glasses are largely sold out ahead of the celestial spectacle this week.

But members of the public have been warned that counterfeit glasses and other alternative ways of seeing the eclipse could lead to harm.

The caution follows warnings from eye doctors, who emphasise that looking straight at the Sun for even brief periods can cause permanent vision damage.

On August 12, the Moon will obscure over 90 per cent of the Sun between 6.17pm and 8.06pm, representing the greatest coverage seen above the UK since 1999.

Specialists stress that only ISO 12312-2 certified glasses offer safe protection. However, approved products are largely sold out, with remaining options requiring hefty delivery fees for timely arrival.

Experts have warned that so-called eclipse glasses that do not carry the safety standards, or ordinary sunglasses, no matter how dark, should never be worn to view an eclipse, as they reduce glare, making it feel more comfortable to look at the Sun for longer, but still allow harmful solar radiation to reach the retina.

Following the 1999 total solar eclipse, the Royal College of Ophthalmologists reported around 70 cases of people experiencing vision problems after watching the eclipse.

open image in gallery Specialists stress that only ISO 12312-2 certified glasses offer safe protection. ( AFP/Getty )

Around 40% had looked at it for less than a minute.

Mohamed Elalfy, a consultant ophthalmologist and president of the Royal College of Ophthalmologists, said: “The safest way to enjoy the eclipse is to observe it indirectly, such as by watching a live broadcast.

“Looking directly at the Sun during a solar eclipse can cause damage to the retina, potentially damaging the cells responsible for sharp central vision.

“Crucially, the retina has no pain receptors, so people will not feel the damage as it happens.

“Symptoms may only become apparent several hours later and can include blurred vision, a central blind or dark spot, distorted vision, reduced colour perception and increased sensitivity to light.

“While some people recover over weeks or months, others can be left with permanent visual impairment.”

Kyla Black, Boots Opticians director of optical practice, urged parents to be “particularly careful” letting their children view the eclipse, and warned some DIY filters can also be dangerous.

“If you’re purchasing specially made eclipse glasses, make sure to double check that they are undamaged before use as even a glimpse of damage could have an impact on your eyesight,” she said.

“It’s a common myth that wearing multiple pairs of sunglasses can protect you from any harmful UV light – this is untrue and should be avoided at all costs as only purpose-built eclipse glasses can allow you to watch an eclipse.”

open image in gallery Special glasses are needed for safely viewing the eclipse. ( AFP/Getty )

Ms Black added: “Although a fun idea for many may be to make DIY filters and pinhole projectors out of cereal boxes, this can also be dangerous.

“Objects such as smoked glass, colour film, floppy disks, X-ray film, and dark sunglasses are unable to block invisible infrared and ultraviolet rays, potentially leading to damage to your eyesight.

“Budding astronomers who will be looking through cameras, binoculars or telescopes at the eclipse must make sure they have approved solar filters attached.

“If you’re not sure your telescope does, then contact the maker of the product to ensure you know you’ll be safe.”

The Royal Observatory Greenwich also warned the public that regular sunglasses are not a safe enough method to view the cosmic phenomenon.

Imo Bell, a planetarium astronomer at the observatory, previously told the Press Association: “It’s not a total eclipse, but over 90% is really exciting.

“We’re not going to get one this good for a really long time.

“So, it’s important not to miss it, and to be prepared.

open image in gallery Celestron solar eclipse glasses on sale at the Royal Observatory Greenwich, south-east London, ahead of the solar eclipse on August 12 ( Jordan Pettitt/PA )

“You can’t just go out and expect to have a look, because it’s really dangerous for your eyes.

“So, you can use solar eclipse glasses, which are very, very different from sunglasses – they block out so much light that you can’t see anything through them except the Sun, because that’s how much light they need to block for the damaging light of the Sun to be safe to view.

“Ideally a solar telescope is an amazing way to witness it, and if you don’t have one of them then you can look into whether your local astronomy society is doing any events.

“And if all else fails, you can project the image of the eclipse using a household item like a colander which has lots of holes in – point the colander towards the Sun with your back facing it, and in the shadow of the colander you’ll be able to see the eclipse in the holes, which is really cool.”

In an added bonus for stargazers, the annual Perseid meteor shower reaches its peak on the night of August 12-13.

The shower is produced as Earth ploughs through a stream of dust left behind by Comet Swift–Tuttle.

Each tiny grain strikes Earth’s atmosphere at about 60 kilometres per second, burning up in a brief flash that takes the appearance of a shooting star.

Cricket governing bodies in Scotland and the Netherlands have strongly criticised the planned restructuring of next year’s 50-over World Cup, claiming that the proposed changes "risk weakening the integrity and credibility of international cricket".

At a board meeting in Edinburgh last month, the International Cricket Council (ICC) revealed that the central phase of the tournament in southern Africa will feature 12 nations split into two groups of six.

Although 14 sides remain involved, the competition will begin with an initial round featuring the three lowest-seeded qualifiers, with just a single team reaching the main group stage.

A preliminary qualifying tournament will run from 22 February until 23 March next year, with the top team advancing directly and those in second, third and fourth entering the opening round.

Cricket Scotland and the Royal Dutch Cricket Association (KNCB) released a joint statement expressing that they were "deeply disappointed" with the ICC’s move, announced under 18 months before the event begins.

open image in gallery Australia won the last 50-over World Cup in 2023 ( Getty )

The statement declared: "At a time when cricket is seeking to expand its reach, attract new audiences and strengthen its position on the international sporting landscape, reducing meaningful opportunities for emerging nations sends entirely the wrong message.

"We have significant concerns about both the impact of these changes and the process through which they have been introduced.

"The changes risk weakening the integrity and credibility of international cricket, and only highlight the importance of strong governance, transparent decision-making and effective engagement with members."

In the men’s ODI rankings, Scotland and the Netherlands are currently placed 13th and 14th respectively.

Monday’s statement follows similar concerns raised by the World Cricketers’ Association over the overhaul, though Cricket Scotland and the KNCB stressed they are "fully committed to working constructively with the ICC and fellow members to strengthen the global game".

The governing bodies added: "Following the announcement of the changes, Cricket Scotland, the KNCB and other associate members met twice with the ICC, seeking official written communication on the changes and greater clarity around the processes involved.

"We also requested positive action to strengthen future operational decision-making and an invitation to bilateral planning meetings with full members.

"Since the second meeting more than two weeks ago, there has been no further response from the ICC, which is disappointing and disrespectful given the significance of the issues raised."
